summary: Alfonso Graziano presents a two-agent pattern for building AI agents: a coding agent (Claude Code) acts as the builder, iteratively improving a product agent that ships to clients. The talk addresses two problem classes: bad performance on evals and bad performance on live data. For eval performance, he introduces golden datasets co-developed with SMEs, scorers that produce an accuracy baseline, and AutoAgent—an iterative loop inspired by Karpathy's auto-research. Each iteration creates a branch, forms a hypothesis targeting one failure class, updates the agent, runs evals, generates a reports.md file, updates a global memory file, and either commits improvements or rolls back regressions. A naive Mastra agent improved from 18% to 83% in ~10 iterations; a production agent improved from 67% to 86% without cheating, by finding edge cases, improving system prompts, tool descriptions, and tool logic. For live data, the workflow collects real user traces with thumbs up/down feedback and SME trace annotations, downloads them as JSON, and runs a coding-agent skill that clusters failure modes, performs adversarial review and root cause analysis, and produces a markdown report. SMEs triage, validate, and prioritize clusters; confirmed failures are fixed by the coding agent and added to the golden dataset as regression tests. Both pipelines depend on Harness Engineering, which Alfonso details in closing: a spec-driven environment where every failure mode becomes a spec for expected behavior, quality gates including linting, unit tests, evals, and LLM code review, context engineering to give the agent the right context, and observability so teams are not blind in production and the coding agent can fix bugs once found. He invites listeners to reach out on LinkedIn to discuss agent-building challenges.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Building AI agents is a systems problem; the core pattern uses two agents: a coding agent as builder and a product agent as shipped artifact.

AutoAgent iteratively improves agents by creating branches, forming hypotheses, running evals, updating memory and reports, and rolling back regressions—improving a naive agent from 18% to 83% and a production agent from 67% to 86%.

Live data optimization collects real user feedback and SME trace annotations, clusters failure modes via a coding-agent skill, performs root cause analysis, and produces a markdown report for SME triage.
Confirmed failure modes from live data are folded back into the golden dataset as regression tests, closing the loop between production feedback and eval suites.
Human-in-the-loop is critical at every stage: structuring the initial agent, enforcing constraints, reviewing promising hypotheses, and triaging failure clusters.

Harness Engineering provides a spec-driven environment, quality gates (linting, unit tests, evals, LLM code review), context engineering, and observability so coding agents can reliably change code and fix production bugs.
Observability is essential: without knowing what happens in production, teams are blind and the coding agent cannot fix bugs once found.
A coding agent can fix an entire suite of issues with a single prompt when given sufficient context and the ability to test changes against regression traces.
Understand the two-agent pattern: coding agent as builder and product agent as shipped artifact
Learn how golden datasets and scorers establish baselines for non-deterministic system evaluation

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Alfonso Graziano introduces himself as a tech lead at NearForm working on AI agentic projects, supporting teams adopting AI-native engineering, and author of the O'Reilly book Learning AI Native Software Engineering.

sections.title: AI Agent Challenges and Definition
sections.summary: Discusses the high cost of AI agents including hallucinations, non-determinism, latency, and cost. Defines an agent as an LLM inside an agentic loop connected to tools and context retrieval, with observability and evals as additional concerns.

sections.title: Problem Classes and Golden Dataset
sections.summary: Introduces two problem classes: bad performance on evals and bad performance on live data. Explains the golden dataset developed with SMEs defining expected inputs and outputs, and scorers that evaluate the dataset with the LLM to produce an accuracy number.

sections.title: Naive Agent Example and Eval Results
sections.summary: Shows a simple Mastra-based agent called 'mad agent' with no tools and a naive evaluator checking if LLM output contains ground truth. The eval suite yields only 18% pass rate since most questions require tools or external context.

sections.title: Agent Failure Modes
sections.summary: Identifies common failure modes: missing the right tools, wrong or incomplete system prompts, and inadequate context retrieval. Notes context retrieval is usually implemented as tools that must be provided securely.

sections.title: Karpathy's Auto-Research Inspiration
sections.summary: References Andrej Karpathy's auto-research, which demonstrated a coding agent tweaking deep learning hyperparameters and Python code to improve model accuracy over multiple experiments.

sections.title: AutoAgent: Applying Auto-Research to AI Agents
sections.summary: Introduces AutoAgent, applying the auto-research concept to AI agents. The coding agent (Claude Code) writes the product agent's code, runs evals, and iteratively improves the agent. Results: naive agent improved from 18% to 83% in ~10 iterations, and +10% on an already-optimized production agent.

sections.title: How AutoAgent Works and Human-in-the-Loop
sections.summary: Explains the loop: coding agent builds the agent, target agent provides feedback via evals and traces. Human-in-the-loop structures the initial agent and enforces constraints such as never updating golden datasets or scorers to pass evals.

sections.title: Optimization Job and Loop Execution
sections.summary: Describes creating a markdown optimization job defining objectives, target repo, and metrics. The loop generates baseline data, forms hypotheses targeting one problem class at a time, updates the agent, re-runs evals, and either commits improvements or rolls back regressions.

sections.title: AutoAgent Iteration Mechanics and Branch Workflow
sections.summary: Details each iteration: create a branch, form a hypothesis, change the agent, run evals, generate reports.md, update a global memory file, and continue from the branch if metrics improved or roll back if they regressed. The agent reads memory and reports to form new hypotheses. A full changelog of improvements and regressions is built. Humans can review promising-but-failed hypotheses and steer the agent.

sections.title: Production Agent Improvement Example
sections.summary: Shows a real production agent that improved from 67% baseline to 86% in ~10 iterations without cheating. The agent found edge cases, improved system prompts, tool descriptions, and fixed tool logic. This agent is now running in production.

sections.title: Live Data Problem Class and Feedback Collection
sections.summary: Introduces the second problem class: bad performance on live data from real users, beta testers, and SMEs. Feedback mechanisms include thumbs up/down with comments and SME trace annotation where experts review inputs, outputs, tool calls, and agent behavior to provide feedback on expected vs actual performance.

sections.title: Live Data Analysis Workflow and Clustering
sections.summary: Describes collecting traces with feedback as JSON (e.g., 114 traces), running a coding-agent skill that clusters failure modes, performs adversarial review and root cause analysis using access to agent code and trace details, and produces a markdown report with positive/negative feedback, negative rate, and proposed fixes with trace IDs and root causes.

sections.title: Triage, Validation, and Golden Dataset Integration
sections.summary: SMEs triage and validate failure clusters, then prioritize: fix now, fix later, or discard (false positives, intended behaviors, low-value feedback). Confirmed failure modes are added to the golden dataset and eval suite as regression tests. Report generation frequency is roughly once per sprint, depending on trace volume.

sections.title: Harness Engineering Overview
sections.summary: Explains that both AutoAgent and the live data pipeline depend on Harness Engineering: building constraints, tasks, feedback loops, and governance around coding agents so they can reliably change code, validate their own changes, and propose new changes when outcomes fall short.

sections.title: Harness Engineering Specifics and Conclusion
sections.summary: Details specific Harness Engineering mechanisms: a spec-driven environment where every failure mode becomes a spec for expected behavior; quality gates including linting, unit tests, evals, and LLM code review; context engineering to give the agent the right context; and observability so teams are not blind in production and the coding agent can fix bugs once found. Alfonso closes by inviting listeners to reach out on LinkedIn to discuss agent-building challenges and share experiences.

demonstrations: Naive Mastra-based agent with no tools achieving 18% eval pass rate
AutoAgent loop improving naive agent from 18% to 83% in ~10 iterations
AutoAgent improving a production agent from 67% to 86% in ~10 iterations without cheating
Branch-per-hypothesis workflow with rollback on regression and a full changelog of improvements and regressions
Live data workflow: user feedback (thumbs up/down), trace collection as JSON (114 traces example), clustering analysis, markdown report with failure clusters
Coding-agent skill for clustering traces, adversarial review, and root cause analysis producing a markdown report
Example failure cluster: small markdown formatting failure where URLs are not hyperlinked, with trace IDs, user feedback, and possible root causes
limitations: The 18% to 83% improvement was on a naive agent without tools, making improvement relatively easy
Live data from real users can be wider and messier than eval data, representing a distinct failure class
Non-determinism, latency, cost, and hallucinations remain inherent problems with AI agents
The coding agent could game evals by modifying golden datasets or scorers if not explicitly constrained
Failure clusters from live data may be false positives, intended behaviors, or low-value feedback requiring human judgment to discard
Report generation frequency depends on trace volume and use case; too many traces may require splitting into multiple reports
Without observability, teams are blind in production and cannot enable the coding agent to fix bugs once found
